title: Idli batter, curd and bread: how tiny living beings make our food

summary.text: Idli batter left on the counter overnight rises to nearly double its size and smells a little sour. Nobody added anything to it. Microbes, living beings too small to see, ate the sugars in the batter and made the bubbles. Your child tests what yeast needs to make gas, and what milk needs to turn into curd, with a fair test, a results table and a line graph. They find out how bacteria and yeast make idli, curd, dosa and bread, and how to tell fermented food from spoiled food. They learn how Louis Pasteur showed that living microbes do the work. They also meet the microbes inside us, in the soil and in medicines like penicillin.
summary.art: A steel container of idli batter on a kitchen counter in the morning, risen to the brim with bubbles on top, beside a mark showing where the batter was the evening before.

intro.hook: Look at a bowl of idli batter in the morning. Last night it was flat and thick. Now it is full of bubbles and has climbed up the sides. What made the bubbles?
intro.text: Nobody blew into it, and nobody stirred it all night. Something alive was working in the batter while your family slept. Microbes, tiny living beings too small to see, were eating the sugars in the rice and dal. As they ate, they made a gas. The sticky batter trapped the gas, and the batter rose. In this unit you find out who the microbes are, what they eat, and how warm they like it. You test it yourself with a bottle and a balloon, and with a cup of milk.
intro.art: Two photographs side by side: flat idli batter in a steel bowl in the evening, and the same bowl in the morning, full of bubbles and risen to the rim.

outcomes: I can explain that fermentation is done by living microbes that eat sugar and make gas, acid or alcohol.
I can say which microbes set curd and which make idli batter and bread rise, and what each one makes.
I can run a fair test that changes one thing at a time, record the results in a table and draw a line graph.
I can explain why microbes need food, water and the right warmth, and why too much heat kills them.
I can tell fermented food from spoiled food, and say when food must be thrown away.
I can name other jobs microbes do for us, in our bodies, in the soil and in medicines.
I can describe how Louis Pasteur showed that living microbes cause fermentation.

terms.meaning: A living being too small to see without a microscope. Bacteria, yeast and moulds are microbes.
terms.example: One drop of curd holds millions of microbes.
terms.art: A spoon of curd with a circle zoomed in to show many tiny rod-shaped bacteria.

terms.meaning: Microbes made of one small cell. Bacteria are found almost everywhere, and many are harmless or helpful.
terms.example: Lactic acid bacteria turn milk into curd.
terms.art: Rod-shaped and round bacteria drawn big, with a ruler showing they are a few thousandths of a millimetre long.

terms.meaning: Fungi are living beings that take in food from whatever they grow on. Mushrooms, moulds and yeast are fungi.
terms.example: Yeast, a single-celled fungus, makes bread dough rise.
terms.art: A mushroom, a patch of mould on bread, and a single yeast cell, each labelled fungus.

terms.meaning: A fungus with one round cell that eats sugar and makes carbon dioxide gas and alcohol.
terms.example: Yeast in dosa or bread dough makes the bubbles that make it soft.
terms.art: A yeast cell budding a smaller cell, like a bump growing on a ball.

terms.meaning: When microbes eat the sugars in food and change them into gas, acid or alcohol.
terms.example: Idli batter ferments overnight and rises.
terms.art: A bowl of batter with tiny microbes eating sugar and bubbles of gas rising.

terms.meaning: An invisible gas with no smell. People and other animals breathe it out. Yeast and bacteria make it when they ferment food.
terms.example: The bubbles in idli batter and in a fizzy drink are carbon dioxide.
terms.art: Bubbles rising from a yeast and sugar mixture inside a clear glass.

terms.meaning: A mild acid that bacteria make from the sugar in milk. It gives curd its sour taste.
terms.example: Curd is sour because of lactic acid.
terms.art: A spoon of curd with a label pointing to the sour taste, and a diagram of a sugar molecule changing into acid.

terms.meaning: A small amount of food that already has the right microbes in it, used to begin fermenting a new batch.
terms.example: A spoonful of old curd added to warm milk is the starter for new curd.
terms.art: A spoon of curd being stirred into a steel pot of warm milk.

terms.meaning: A stretchy protein in wheat flour. In dough it forms a net that traps gas.
terms.example: A soft bun is full of holes where gas was trapped in gluten.
terms.art: A stretched piece of dough pulled thin, with tiny gas bubbles held inside.

terms.meaning: Alive but resting, with almost no activity. Dry yeast in a packet is dormant.
terms.example: Dry yeast wakes up when you add warm water and sugar.
terms.art: A packet of dry yeast on one side and a foamy glass of yeast and sugar water on the other.

terms.meaning: When unwanted microbes grow in food and make it unsafe or unpleasant to eat.
terms.example: A chapati kept damp for three days grows mould and must be thrown away.
terms.art: A closed box with a chapati covered in blue-green and white mould.

terms.meaning: To heat milk or juice to kill harmful microbes, without cooking it. The word comes from Louis Pasteur.
terms.example: Packet milk is pasteurised before it is sold.
terms.art: A pan of milk on a stove with a thermometer, beside a portrait of Louis Pasteur.

terms.meaning: A medicine that kills bacteria or stops them growing. Many antibiotics were first found in moulds and soil microbes.
terms.example: Penicillin comes from a mould called Penicillium.
terms.art: A petri dish with a mould in the middle and a clear ring around the mould where bacteria cannot grow.

terms.meaning: A living being that breaks down dead plants and animals into simple parts that go back into the soil.
terms.example: Fungi and bacteria in the soil turn fallen leaves into soil.
terms.art: A fallen leaf slowly turning into dark soil, with mushrooms and tiny microbes drawn on it.

terms.meaning: The part of an experiment that is left without the thing you are testing, so you can compare the other parts with it.
terms.example: In the yeast test, the bottle with no yeast is the control.
terms.art: Four bottles in a row with a label on one that says no yeast: the control.

terms.meaning: The trillions of bacteria that live in your intestines. Most are harmless, and many help break down food.
terms.example: Gut bacteria break down fibre that your own body cannot digest.
terms.art: A cut-away of a child's belly showing the long coiled intestine with tiny bacteria inside.

explanations.concept: Fermentation: microbes eat sugar and make something new
explanations.definition: Fermentation is when microbes eat the sugars in food and change them into other things, such as carbon dioxide gas, acid or alcohol.
explanations.description: A microbe is a living being too small to see. Microbes need food to live, just as you do. Many of them eat sugar. When yeast eat sugar, they make carbon dioxide gas and a little alcohol. When some bacteria eat sugar, they make acid. These new substances are what change the food. The gas makes dough and batter rise. The acid makes curd sour and thick. People did not invent fermentation. They noticed it, thousands of years ago, and learned how to look after it. Fermented foods are among the oldest foods people eat. Today we know which microbes are doing the work in many of them.
examples: Yeast fermenting sugar in dough makes carbon dioxide and a little alcohol, and the dough rises.
Bacteria fermenting milk sugar make lactic acid, and the milk turns into curd.
Palm sap, called neera, ferments within hours in the heat. It turns into toddy because yeast change the sugar in the sap into alcohol.
explanations.art: A diagram: sugar going into a microbe on the left, and gas bubbles, acid and alcohol coming out on the right.

explanations.concept: Yeast: the fungus behind bread, dosa and appam
explanations.definition: Yeast is a fungus made of a single round cell. Yeast eat sugar and make carbon dioxide gas and alcohol.
explanations.description: A yeast cell is about one hundredth of a millimetre wide. You would need to line up about one hundred of them to cross one millimetre. A single gram of baker's yeast holds billions of cells. Dry yeast in a packet is dormant, which means alive but resting. Warm water and sugar wake the cells up. They sense the sugar, take it in and begin to grow. A yeast cell grows a small bump called a bud. The bud gets bigger and then breaks off as a new cell. In warm sugary dough, yeast can double in number in about an hour and a half. All the while they make carbon dioxide gas, and the gas makes the dough rise.
examples: Bread, pav, buns, naan and kulcha are often made with yeast.
Appam batter is traditionally risen with toddy, which carries yeast, and many families now use a pinch of dry yeast.
In the bottle and balloon test, the balloon fills with the carbon dioxide that the yeast make.
explanations.art: Three drawings in a row: a dormant yeast cell, the same cell with a small bud, and the bud breaking off as a new cell.

explanations.concept: Curd: bacteria turn milk sugar into acid
explanations.definition: Curd is milk that has been changed by lactic acid bacteria. The bacteria eat the sugar in milk, called lactose, and make lactic acid.
explanations.description: Milk is mostly water, with sugar, fat and protein dissolved or floating in it. The main protein is called casein. When you add a spoonful of old curd to warm milk, you add millions of lactic acid bacteria. They eat the milk sugar and make lactic acid. The milk slowly becomes more sour. When there is enough acid, the casein sticks together into a soft net. The net holds the water inside it, and the milk sets into curd. That is why curd is thick and tastes sour. A spoonful of old curd is called a starter because it starts the next batch. It works because the bacteria in the starter are alive. Plain boiled milk with no starter stays milk.
examples: Warm milk with one spoon of old curd sets overnight in most Indian kitchens.
Buttermilk, lassi, raita and kadhi all begin with curd.
Paneer is not made by bacteria. It is made by adding lemon juice or vinegar, which are acids, to hot milk.
explanations.art: A cut-away of milk with sugar, fat and protein drawn as dots, then the same milk with bacteria making acid and the protein joining into a net that holds water.

explanations.concept: Idli and dosa batter: a team of microbes
explanations.definition: Idli and dosa batter ferments because many kinds of bacteria and yeast eat the sugars in the batter. They arrive on the rice, the dal and the utensils, and from the air.
explanations.description: Nobody adds yeast or bacteria to most home-made batter. Microbes are already on the urad dal, the rice and the grinder. Once the batter is mixed and kept in a warm place, they begin to eat. Scientists have studied idli batter in many kitchens. They found that a bacterium called Leuconostoc is often the main gas-maker, with other lactic acid bacteria and some yeasts working alongside. The mix is slightly different in every kitchen. The microbes make carbon dioxide gas and lactic acid. The urad dal makes the batter sticky, so the gas stays trapped in tiny bubbles. Steaming then kills the microbes and sets the idli into a soft, spongy cake.
examples: The batter rises in a few hours in a warm Chennai kitchen.
The same batter can take a whole day in a cool Shimla winter.
Dosa, uttapam and many other batters work in the same way.
explanations.art: A rice and dal batter with bubbles, showing a few bacteria and yeast cells inside one bubble, and a steamer with idlis next to it.

explanations.concept: What microbes need: food, water and the right warmth
explanations.definition: Microbes grow best with food, water and the right warmth. Cold slows them down, and too much heat kills them.
explanations.description: Every living being needs food, water and a place to live, and microbes are the same. Most helpful microbes in the kitchen grow best at about the warmth of a warm room, around 30 to 40 degrees Celsius. In the fridge, at about 4 degrees, they still live but grow very slowly. That is why the fridge keeps food fresh for longer. Above about 50 degrees, most of them begin to die. At the temperature of boiling water, most of them are killed in minutes. That is why we boil milk before making curd, and why we cool it down before adding the starter. If the milk is too hot, the bacteria in the starter die. The rule is the same for yeast.
examples: Curd sets overnight in a warm kitchen, but takes much longer on a cold winter morning.
Dry yeast stirred into boiling water dies and does not make bubbles.
Leftover cooked rice kept in the fridge stays safe for longer than rice left out in the heat.
explanations.art: A thermometer with a green zone in the middle for warm, a blue zone at the bottom for the fridge, and a red zone at the top for hot, with a small microbe drawn in each zone.

explanations.concept: Trapping the gas: why dough and batter rise
explanations.definition: Dough and batter rise when carbon dioxide gas made by microbes is trapped inside something sticky or stretchy.
explanations.description: A gas made inside a runny liquid would simply bubble up and escape. To make bread or idli rise, the gas must be held in. Wheat dough holds it with gluten. Gluten is a stretchy protein that forms a net when you knead flour and water. The gas pushes into the net and stretches it, like blowing up a balloon. Urad dal batter holds the gas because dal makes the batter thick and sticky. Rice alone would not hold it so well. When you steam the idli or bake the bread, the gas expands and the heat sets the sticky net. It becomes firm and keeps its shape with all the holes inside.
examples: Bread cut open shows many holes where gas was trapped.
Idli, dhokla and appam have a soft inside full of tiny holes.
A balloon over a bottle of yeast and sugar water catches the gas and shows how much was made.
explanations.art: A stretching dough net holding gas bubbles, next to a balloon stretching as it fills.

explanations.definition: Fermented food has been changed by microbes that we want. Spoiled food has been changed by microbes that we do not want.
explanations.description: Both kinds of food are changed by microbes. The difference is which microbes, and whether we chose them. In curd and idli batter, the helpful microbes make acid. The acid makes it hard for harmful microbes to grow. That is one reason curd stays safe for days. Spoilage is different. It happens when unwanted microbes grow, often because food was left damp and warm for too long. Fuzzy mould, a slimy surface, an unpleasant smell or odd colours are signs of spoilage. If you are not sure, do not taste it. Throw it away. Never cut off the mould and eat the rest, because mould threads can spread deep into soft food.
examples: A sour smell from batter or curd is normal.
Fuzzy green, white, black or pink patches on bread, chapati or curd mean it must be thrown away.
Leftover rice left in a warm kitchen all day can grow bacteria that cause food poisoning.
explanations.art: Two bowls: one of fresh sour curd and one of mouldy bread, with a tick on the curd and a cross on the bread.

explanations.definition: Many regions of India have their own fermented foods, made with local grains, vegetables, soybeans, milk and fruit.
explanations.description: People in every part of India have learned to make food with microbes. In the south, idli, dosa and appam use fermented rice and dal batter. In Gujarat, dhokla is made from fermented gram flour batter. In Punjab, kanji is a sour drink made by fermenting black carrots in water with mustard. In Sikkim, kinema is made from fermented soybeans, and in Manipur hawaijar is made the same way. In Nagaland, akhuni is a fermented soybean paste. Gundruk, fermented leafy greens, is eaten in Sikkim and the hills nearby. Many of these foods keep well without a fridge. They also taste different from the plain ingredients they came from.
examples: Idli, dosa, appam and uttapam from the south.
Dhokla from Gujarat, and kanji from Punjab.
Kinema from Sikkim, hawaijar from Manipur and akhuni from Nagaland, all made from soybeans.
explanations.art: A map of India with small drawings of idli, appam, dhokla, kanji, kinema, hawaijar and akhuni in their regions.

explanations.description: Your intestines hold trillions of bacteria, more than the number of stars you could count in a clear night sky. Most are harmless, and many help you. Some break down fibre that your own body cannot digest. Some make vitamin K. Others take up space so that harmful bacteria have less room to grow. Scientists are now studying how much these bacteria affect our health, our mood and even our weight. This is a young science, and results are still being checked. Many claims in advertisements go further than the evidence. What scientists agree on is that a gut full of many kinds of bacteria is usually a healthy gut, and that eating many kinds of plant food helps.
examples: Gut bacteria break down some of the fibre in dal, vegetables and fruit.
Curd and buttermilk contain living bacteria, and scientists are still studying what these do in the gut.
A baby picks up many of her first gut bacteria from her mother, and from the people and the world around her.
explanations.art: A cut-away of a child's belly with the intestine full of many different-coloured tiny bacteria.

perspectives.explanation: Gut bacteria clearly help with digestion and may affect health in many ways. We should study them carefully, and be honest about what we do not know yet.

Many products sold as good for gut bacteria have not been tested well. Some studies were small or have not been repeated. A person should be careful before spending money or changing medical treatment.

explanations.definition: Microbes also break down dead plants and animals in the soil, clean water, and make medicines.
explanations.description: Without microbes, the world would be buried under dead leaves and animals. Bacteria and fungi in soil and compost break dead material into simple parts that plants take up again. Sewage plants use microbes to clean dirty water. In 1928, Alexander Fleming noticed that a Penicillium mould on a dish had killed the bacteria around the mould. This led to penicillin, the first antibiotic. Dorothy Hodgkin worked out the shape of the penicillin molecule in 1945. In 1954, India began making penicillin at Hindustan Antibiotics in Pimpri, near Pune. Antibiotics kill bacteria, but they do not work against illnesses caused by viruses, such as colds and flu.
examples: Compost heaps get warm because decomposers are working hard.
Penicillin comes from the Penicillium mould.
Vinegar is made when bacteria turn alcohol into acid.
explanations.art: A compost heap with a thermometer showing a warm centre, and next to it a petri dish with mould and a clear ring around the mould.

explanations.concept: Choosing our microbes: pasteurised milk and starters
explanations.definition: Pasteurising milk kills most harmful microbes by gentle heating. After that, we choose the microbes we want by adding a starter.
explanations.description: Raw milk from a cow can carry harmful bacteria. Boiling the milk kills most of them. Packet milk is pasteurised in a factory, which means it is heated just enough to kill the harmful ones. Louis Pasteur showed in the 1860s that gentle heating could stop wine from going sour, by killing the microbes that spoil it. The word pasteurise comes from his name. Later, dairies used the same idea for milk. After heating, the milk has almost no microbes left. We then add a spoonful of curd, which has the lactic acid bacteria we want. These bacteria grow fast, make acid, and leave little room for others. Cooks have used the same idea for centuries, long before anyone knew why it worked. They kept a bit of the last batch to begin the next.
examples: A kitchen starter can be kept going for many years, all from one batch of curd.
Packet curd is made in a dairy with chosen bacteria added to pasteurised milk.
Sourdough bread uses a starter that has been fed with flour and water for days, years or even centuries.
explanations.art: Three steps drawn left to right: milk being heated in a pan, the milk cooling with a thermometer, and a spoon of starter curd being stirred in.

agreed.text: Fermentation is done by living microbes, such as yeast and bacteria.
agreed.evidence: In 1857 and 1860 Louis Pasteur showed that fermentation stopped when the living microbes were killed, and started when they were added.

agreed.text: The gas in bread dough and idli batter is carbon dioxide made by microbes eating sugar.
agreed.evidence: The gas can be caught in a balloon, and it puts out a lit match. Without the microbes, no gas appears.

agreed.text: Microbes grow fastest when it is warm, slow down when it is cold and die when it is very hot.
agreed.evidence: Curd, batter and yeast tests have been done many times at different temperatures, and each time they show the same pattern.

agreed.text: Lactic acid bacteria make milk sour and thick by turning milk sugar into lactic acid.
agreed.evidence: The acid can be measured, and milk with the bacteria killed does not set.

agreed.text: Most microbes are harmless or helpful. Only a small fraction cause disease.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have counted the microbes in soil, water and our bodies, and found that far more are harmless than harmful.

agreed.text: Fuzzy mould on soft food means the food should be thrown away.
agreed.evidence: Mould sends thin threads deep into soft food, and some moulds make poisons that cooking does not remove.

challenging.claim: Idli batter rises because of the grinding, or because of baking soda.
challenging.who: Some people, and some recipe books.
challenging.for: A fresh batter can puff up a little from air whipped in during grinding. Some quick idli recipes use baking soda or fruit salt.
challenging.against: Batter ground and left in a cold fridge stays flat. Batter left in a warm place rises over hours, and smells sour. That points to living microbes, not air or a powder.

challenging.claim: All microbes are germs, and we should kill them all.
challenging.for: Some microbes do cause illness, and washing hands and cleaning wounds matter.
challenging.against: Most microbes are harmless, and many help. Curd, idli, bread, soil and our own gut depend on them. Killing all the microbes would also kill the helpful ones.

challenging.claim: Fermented food is just food that has gone bad.
challenging.who: Some people who have never made it.
challenging.for: Both fermented food and spoiled food are changed by microbes, and both can smell sour.
challenging.against: In fermented food, helpful microbes make acid that keeps harmful ones away. In spoiled food, unwanted microbes take over. People have eaten fermented food safely for thousands of years.

challenging.claim: Eating curd or probiotic drinks every day is needed to keep your gut healthy.
challenging.for: Curd has living bacteria and is a good food. Some studies find small benefits for some people.
challenging.against: Many probiotic drinks have not been well tested. Your gut gets bacteria from many foods and from the world around you. A varied diet with plenty of plant food matters more than any one product.

challenging.claim: Yeast and bacteria are only tiny machines.
challenging.for: Their responses can be explained by chemistry: sugar arrives, certain genes switch on, and the cell responds.
challenging.against: Bacteria and yeast sense food and poisons, swim or grow towards food and away from poison, and signal to each other. The same chemistry is what any living being uses to sense and respond, including us.

big_questions.q: When you make curd, who makes it: you, or the bacteria?
big_questions.hint: Think about what you did in the Curd Test, and what happened in cup D, which got no starter.

big_questions.q: If a spoon of curd is full of living bacteria, are we eating a food or a community?
big_questions.hint: Think about what happens to the bacteria in your stomach and gut.

big_questions.q: Why do bacteria in curd stay in the milk and not take over the whole kitchen?
big_questions.hint: Think about food, warmth and the acid they make.

big_questions.q: Idli rises differently in every kitchen. Why would two kitchens have different microbes?
big_questions.hint: Think about where microbes come from: the dal, the rice, the grinder, the air.

big_questions.q: A yeast cell senses sugar and takes it in. What might sugar mean to a yeast cell?
big_questions.hint: Think about how a yeast cell finds, takes in and uses sugar.

big_questions.q: Are microbes too small to matter, or are they the foundation of everything else?
big_questions.hint: Think about what would happen to soil, food and us without them.

big_questions.q: Who was the first person to find out that a spoon of curd makes more curd?
big_questions.hint: Nobody knows. How could people discover it without microscopes or even words for microbes?

big_questions.q: If a bacterium splits into two, which one is the parent and which one is the child?
big_questions.hint: Think about what each new cell inherits and what is left of the first cell.

story.title: The Batter That Would Not Rise
story.note: A made-up story. The science in it is real. Idli batter rises because microbes make gas, and it rises slowly or not at all when it is cold. A spoonful of batter from an earlier day brings in microbes that are already active.
text: In December, Thara and her mother travelled from Chennai to Shimla to stay with Reena Aunty. Thara was in Class 4. She had never seen snow, and she had never felt a kitchen so cold. Her breath made clouds in the air.

On the first evening, Thara and Reena Aunty decided to make idli, for the whole family. Reena Aunty had a mixer and a bag of idli rice. Thara had her grandmother's rule in her head. Three parts rice, one part urad dal. They soaked the rice and dal, ground them, added salt and poured the batter into a big steel pot.
'Now we leave it overnight,' said Thara. 'In the morning it will be double.'
In the morning, the batter was exactly where they had left it. It was flat, and smooth, and a little cold to touch. There were no bubbles.
'I must have ground it wrong,' said Reena Aunty, looking worried.
Raghu Uncle came into the kitchen with his tea. 'Add a pinch of baking soda,' he said. 'My mother always did.' He took a spoon.
'Wait,' said Thara. 'I think the batter is fine.'

Thara thought about what she knew. In Chennai, her grandmother's batter always rose by morning. In Chennai, the kitchen was warm even at night. She remembered how yeast made bubbles in warm sugar water, and not in cold. 'The batter is full of living microbes,' she said. 'They eat the sugar and make the gas. But they eat very slowly when it is cold. I think your kitchen is too cold for them.'
'Microbes,' said Uncle. He looked at the pot. 'You mean there are tiny living things in there?'
'Yes. The dal and the rice are covered in them. They were almost asleep all night. They need a warm place.'
Reena Aunty thought for a moment. 'The oven,' she said. 'If I switch on only the little light inside, it gets warm, like the inside of a cupboard in summer.'

Thara put her hand inside the oven after a few minutes. It felt as warm as a kitchen in Chennai. They put the pot in, closed the door, and left a note on the oven so that nobody would switch on the heat.

That evening, they lifted the lid. The batter had risen right to the top, and the top was covered in tiny bubbles. It smelled a little sour, exactly like her grandmother's kitchen in Chennai. Thara put her ear close, and heard a very quiet fizzing, like tiny bubbles popping.
They steamed the idlis and everyone ate them hot. Raghu Uncle ate four. 'I was wrong about the baking soda,' he said. 'The batter was not broken. It was just cold.'
Thara smiled. 'The batter was alive all the time. It just needed to be warm.'

Before bed, Thara told Reena Aunty one more thing her grandmother did. She always kept a spoonful of the old batter, to stir into the next one. 'She calls it the starter,' said Thara. 'It is already awake.' Reena Aunty found a small steel cup and set a spoonful of batter aside, in the fridge.

Reena Aunty went to bed smiling. Thara stayed in the kitchen a little longer, thinking about the microbes in the batter. They had been eating and making their gas all day. None of them knew about Shimla or Chennai. They only knew warm, and food, and each other.
story.epiphany: The batter was not broken. It was alive, and it was cold.
ask: What would you do if your batter would not rise in a cold house? Why would that work?
How could you check whether a batter has living microbes in it, without tasting it?
Why might a spoonful of yesterday's batter help today's batter rise?
