roots.context: We have tested what yeast and curd bacteria need, and learned how they change our food. Now we ask what this tells us about who does the work, and who we are.

deep_truth.truth: In the Curd Test, milk with a spoon of old curd set. The same milk with no old curd stayed milk. The old curd carried living bacteria, who changed the milk as they ate the sugar in it. A cook only makes the warm, sweet place where they can work.
deep_truth.habit: We say 'I made the curd' and 'the dough rose' as if the cook did all the work. The cook prepared the place. Living beings we cannot see did the changing.
deep_truth.evidence: In the curd test, the cup with a starter set and the cup with no starter stayed liquid. In the yeast test, the bottle with no yeast made no gas. If your own results differ, write them down as they are and test again.

three.who_am_i: Your gut holds trillions of bacteria. You are a home for living beings, and they help you digest your food.
three.what_is_life: Yeast and bacteria sense sugar, grow, split and make more of themselves. They are tiny, and they are alive in the same way you are.
three.what_is_this_world: Most of the living beings on Earth are microbes. They have been working on this planet for billions of years, long before people arrived.

roots.thread: A spoon of starter curd carries bacteria from the last batch, and the batch before that, back through many kitchens. When one bacterium splits in two, no old body is left behind. Both new cells carry the same instructions, in a chain that goes back billions of years. Idli, curd and bread connect you to that long line of living beings, and to the people who kept a spoonful of the last batch for the next.

teachings.teaching: A father asks his son to put salt in water, and to bring the water back the next morning. The salt cannot be seen. But the father asks the son to taste the water from the top, the middle and the bottom, and it is salty everywhere. The father teaches that something unseen can be in everything.
teachings.link: You cannot see the microbes in batter, but you know they are there because of what they do: the bubbles, the sour smell and the rise. Something you cannot see can still be there.

teachings.source: Thich Nhat Hanh, Peace Is Every Step (1991), chapter on interbeing
teachings.teaching: Thich Nhat Hanh asks us to look deeply at a sheet of paper. He says that if you look carefully, you can see a cloud, the sun and a tree in the paper, because the paper could not exist without them. Nothing exists alone.
teachings.link: In a bowl of curd you can find the grass the cow ate, the farmer, the sun and the bacteria. Each one is needed for the curd to exist.

teachings.teaching: Margulis, an American biologist, argued that life has been shaped as much by partnership as by competition. Her work showed that mitochondria, the parts of our cells that release energy, began as free-living bacteria that moved into other cells.
teachings.link: The bacteria in your gut and the mitochondria in your own cells show that bodies are built from living partners.

science.text: Mitochondria, which release energy in every cell of your body, began as free-living bacteria that moved into another cell more than a billion years ago.
How much gut bacteria shape our health and mood is still being studied. Scientists do not yet agree on how large the effects are.

other_view.view: Yeast and bacteria respond to sugar through chemistry. Sugar arrives, certain genes switch on, and the cell grows. They would say this is an automatic process, like our skin healing a cut, and not a feeling or a choice.

practice.title: Listen to the batter
practice.say: Find a bowl of batter that has been fermenting, or a glass of yeast and sugar water. Sit quietly beside it. Bring your ear close to the surface. Listen for a very quiet fizzing, like tiny bubbles popping. Close your eyes and breathe in slowly three times. Smell the faint sourness. Think about the many tiny beings inside, working together right now.
practice.kid: Hold your ear near the bowl. Close your eyes. Listen for a tiny fizz. Breathe in slowly three times. Many tiny beings are working in there.

ask: If a spoon of curd carries the bacteria, is the new curd something new, or the old curd carrying on?
When you eat curd, are you eating a food, or meeting a community?
What might a yeast cell be doing at the moment sugar arrives?
roots.art: A spoon of curd above a bowl of milk with fine lines running back to earlier bowls and earlier kitchens, and tiny bacteria drawn inside the spoon.

games.title: Kitchen Verdict: will the microbes work?
games.context: This is a guessing game. Each card shows a situation in a kitchen. You decide whether the microbes will work well, slow down or stop.

setup.art: Twenty-four cards in a shuffled pile in the middle of a table, with three verdict tokens in front of each player.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards into a pile.

setup.art: One child reading a card aloud, while two others each put a token face down in front of them.
setup.caption: 2. The reader reads a card. Everyone else picks a token.

setup.art: Three tokens turned over together, and the reader turning the card around to show the answer on the back.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the tokens over. The reader shows the back.

printables.title: 24 two-sided cards: a kitchen situation on the front, and the verdict with the reason on the back

items.f: Idli batter, made of rice and dal, is left in a warm kitchen at 30 degrees for 10 hours.
items.b: Works well. It is warm and full of sugars, so the microbes grow fast and the batter rises.

items.f: The same idli batter is left in the fridge overnight.
items.b: Slows down. The microbes are alive in the cold, but they grow very slowly, so the batter hardly rises.

items.f: Dry yeast and sugar are stirred into boiling hot water.
items.b: Stops. Most yeast die in water hotter than about 55 degrees, so no gas is made.

items.f: Dry yeast is stirred into warm water with a teaspoon of sugar.
items.b: Works well. The warmth wakes the yeast, and the sugar is their food. Foam and gas appear in minutes.

items.f: Dry yeast is stirred into ice-cold water with a teaspoon of sugar.
items.b: Slows down. The yeast stay alive in the cold, but they make very little gas.

items.f: Boiled milk is cooled until it is finger-warm, and then a spoonful of curd is stirred in.
items.b: Works well. The living bacteria in the spoonful eat the milk sugar and make lactic acid. The milk sets.

items.f: Boiled milk is cooled until it is finger-warm, and nothing is added to it.
items.b: Stops. With no bacteria added, nothing changes the milk into curd. It stays milk.

items.f: Boiling hot milk, straight off the stove, gets a spoonful of curd stirred in.
items.b: Stops. The heat kills the bacteria in the spoonful, so the milk does not set.

items.f: Idlis are put into a steamer for 12 minutes. Will the microbes in the batter keep making gas?
items.b: Stops. Steam heats the idli past 60 degrees and kills the microbes. The gas already made stays trapped, and the idli sets firm.

items.f: A tray of yeast dough goes into a very hot oven. Will the yeast keep making gas?
items.b: Stops. Yeast die above about 55 degrees. The dough puffs a little more as the gas expands, and then the crust sets.

items.f: A pot of curd sits in the fridge for a week.
items.b: Slows down. The bacteria keep making acid, but very slowly, so the curd only gets a little more sour.

items.f: Yeast dough is left in a cool room at 15 degrees.
items.b: Slows down. The dough will still rise, but it can take many hours.

items.f: It is winter. You stir a spoonful of yesterday's batter into the new batter, and put the pot in a warm cupboard.
items.b: Works well. The old batter brings microbes that are already active, and the warm cupboard helps them work.

items.f: Bread dough is covered with a damp cloth and left in a warm kitchen for one hour.
items.b: Works well. The yeast eat the sugars that come from the flour, and fill the dough with gas.

items.f: A balloon is fitted on a bottle of yeast, sugar and warm water.
items.b: Works well. The yeast make carbon dioxide, and the balloon swells.

items.f: A balloon is fitted on a bottle of yeast and warm water, with no sugar.
items.b: Slows down. The yeast have very little food, so they make only a little gas.

items.f: A tight lid is screwed onto a jar of fermenting batter.
items.b: Works well, so be careful. The microbes keep making gas, and a tight lid can burst. Leave the lid loose.

items.f: Dhokla batter, made with gram flour and sour curd, rests for six hours in a warm kitchen.
items.b: Works well. The bacteria from the curd make gas and acid, and the batter puffs up.

items.f: A packet of dry yeast has been open for a year in a hot cupboard.
items.b: Slows down. Many of the yeast cells have died, so less gas is made. A baker tests a pinch in warm sugar water first.

items.f: A chapati is kept damp in a closed box in a warm kitchen for three days. Will mould grow?
items.b: Works well, for the mould. This is spoilage, not fermentation. Throw the chapati away.

items.f: A glass flask of sugar broth is boiled, then sealed so that no air can get in.
items.b: Stops. Boiling kills the microbes inside, and the seal keeps new ones out. This is what Pasteur found.

items.f: A small spoon of salt goes into idli batter, and the batter is left warm.
items.b: Works well. A little salt gives flavour and does not stop the microbes.

items.f: A big cupful of starter curd, as much as half the milk, goes into warm milk.
items.b: Works well, and fast. More bacteria at the start means the milk sets sooner. It may taste more sour.

items.f: Fresh palm sap, called neera, is left in a clay pot in the warm air for half a day.
items.b: Works well. Yeast turn the sugar in the sap into alcohol within hours, and the neera becomes toddy. Children should not drink it.

printables.title: 12 verdict tokens: four sets of three

rules: Works well means the microbes are growing fast. Slows down means they are alive but working slowly. Stops means they cannot work or are dead.
One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the front aloud. The reader does not show the back.
Every other player puts one verdict token face down. Then everyone turns the tokens over together.
The reader turns the card around and reads the back. Every player whose token matches the verdict at the start of the back scores one point.
With two players, the parent and the child swap roles after every card. The reader never guesses on their own card.
After each card, the reader passes the reader's job to the player on their left.
The game ends when all 24 cards have been read. The player with the most points wins. If there is a tie, the tied players share the win.

flow.do: Cut out the 24 cards and the 12 tokens. Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile. Give each player one token of each kind.
flow.say: These cards show situations in a kitchen. Each player gets three tokens: Works well, Slows down and Stops. We will guess what the microbes do.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards. Each player takes three tokens.
flow.context: This is the first step of Kitchen Verdict. You set up the cards and the tokens.
flow.parent: A grown-up cuts the cards with scissors, or the children cut them with blunt scissors while you watch. If you cannot print, write the 24 cards on small pieces of paper. With one child, you play with them; with 2 to 4 children, the reader changes after every card.

flow.do: Play the first six cards. After each one, read the back aloud. Ask the question below after card three.
flow.say: The reader reads the front. Everyone else chooses a token. Turn the tokens over together. Now the reader reads the back. Who got a point?
flow.kid: The reader reads a card. Pick a token. Turn it over. Check the back.

ask.q: Think of a card where the microbes slowed down or stopped. Why do you think that happened?
good: There were no microbes to begin with.

flow.context: In this step, you play the first six cards and learn how to guess.

flow.do: Play the next eight cards. Swap the reader's job after every card. Keep a tally of points on paper.
flow.say: Keep going. Remember what microbes need: food, water and the right warmth. Too cold slows them. Too hot kills them.
flow.kid: Play on. Remember food, water and warmth. Too cold slows them. Too hot kills them.

ask.q: What did the cards where the microbes stopped have in common?
good: They had no microbes to begin with.

flow.context: In this step, you play the middle of the game and keep score.

flow.do: Play the last ten cards. When the pile is finished, count each player's points.
flow.say: These are the last cards. Think about what the microbes need on each card, and what the temperature is.
flow.kid: Play the last cards. Count your points.
flow.context: In this step, you finish the pile of cards and count the points.

flow.do: Say who won. Ask your child which card surprised them most, and why.
flow.say: Who got the most points? Which card surprised you most? Why did it surprise you?
flow.kid: Who won? Which card surprised you most? Why?
flow.think: Pick one card. What would you change on it to get a different verdict?
flow.context: This is the last step of Kitchen Verdict. You look back at the game.

experiments.title: Yeast Balloon: what do yeast need to make gas?
experiments.question: Which bottle makes the most gas: yeast with sugar and warm water, yeast with no sugar, yeast with sugar in the cold, or sugar with no yeast?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which balloon will fill the most? Which will stay flat? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every bottle is the same size, with 200 millilitres of water and the same kind of balloon. Bottle A has everything. Bottle B has no sugar. Bottle C is kept in the fridge. Bottle D has no yeast. Each bottle differs from A in only one way, so any difference in the balloons comes from that one thing. Bottle D is the control.

materials.item: 4 clean plastic bottles, about 500 millilitres each (empty water bottles are fine)
4 small round balloons, stretched by blowing up and letting down once before you start
3 level teaspoons of instant dry yeast (one small sachet from a kirana or bakery-supply shop, about 7 to 10 grams)
6 level teaspoons of sugar
600 millilitres of warm water, as warm as a comfortable bath for a baby
200 millilitres of cold water from a bottle kept in the fridge
a measuring cup or a tumbler marked at 200 millilitres
a cloth tape measure, or a piece of string and a ruler
a marker pen, a tray, a clock or timer, and the results table

experiments.safety: Use warm water, never hot, because hot water kills yeast and can scald. A grown-up checks the water first. Do not drink anything in the bottles. Keep the balloon away from the mouth, and do not blow into it. Wash hands after handling the yeast water. Keep burst balloon pieces away from children under five, because they can choke on them.
experiments.record: Write the balloon size, in centimetres around the widest part, at 10, 20, 30 and 40 minutes. Then draw a line graph with one line for each bottle. There are no right sizes. Whatever you measure is your result.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you find out what yeast need to make gas. You change one thing at a time, and catch the gas in a balloon.

setup.art: Four bottles in a row labelled A, B, C and D, each with a measuring cup beside it showing 200 millilitres of water.
setup.caption: 1. Put 200 millilitres of water in each bottle. Use cold water in C.

setup.art: Two teaspoons of sugar being stirred into the water in a bottle, and a note showing that bottle B gets no sugar.
setup.caption: 2. Add two teaspoons of sugar to A, C and D. Leave B without sugar.

setup.art: A teaspoon of dry yeast being added to a bottle, with a note that bottle D gets no yeast.
setup.caption: 3. Add one level teaspoon of yeast to A, B and C. Leave D without yeast.

setup.art: A balloon being stretched over the neck of a bottle, with the bottle then placed on a tray, and bottle C placed in a fridge.
setup.caption: 4. Fit a balloon on each bottle. Put C in the fridge. Leave A, B and D on a tray.

setup.art: A child wrapping a cloth tape measure around the widest part of a swollen balloon on a bottle, with a table of numbers beside it.
setup.caption: 5. Every 10 minutes, measure around each balloon and write the number.

flow.do: Show your child the four bottles on the tray, labelled A, B, C and D. Read out what goes in each bottle. Write down their guess and their reason.
flow.say: We will test four bottles. Bottle A gets yeast, sugar and warm water. Bottle B gets yeast and warm water, but no sugar. Bottle C gets yeast and sugar, but stays in the fridge. Bottle D gets sugar and warm water, but no yeast. Which balloon will fill the most? Which will stay flat? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: There are four bottles. A has everything. B has no sugar. C goes in the fridge. D has no yeast. Which balloon fills the most? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Why do you think that bottle will fill the most?
good: Yeast eat sugar to make gas.
It has everything the yeast need.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Write the guesses at the top of the table.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Yeast Balloon test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Pour 200 millilitres of warm water into bottles A, B and D. Pour 200 millilitres of cold water into bottle C. Add two level teaspoons of sugar to A, C and D. Stir each until the sugar disappears.
flow.say: Warm water first, into A, B and D. Cold water goes into C. Now two teaspoons of sugar go into A, C and D, but not into B. Stir until the sugar has dissolved.
flow.kid: Pour 200 millilitres of warm water into A, B and D. Pour cold water into C. Add two teaspoons of sugar to A, C and D. Stir.
flow.parent: Warm means about 40 degrees. You can hold a finger in it for 10 seconds. If it is too hot to hold, let it cool first. Hot water kills the yeast. Roles: with one child, you pour and your child stirs and labels. With 2 to 4 children, each child owns one bottle (A, B, C or D), adds its ingredients and measures its balloon; a grown-up checks the water.

check.q: Why do we leave sugar out of bottle B?
options: To see if yeast make gas without sugar
To make bottle B colder
To save sugar
check.why: Bottle B differs from bottle A in one way only: it has no sugar. If it makes less gas than A, the sugar made the difference.

flow.context: In this step, you set up the water and the sugar. Each bottle gets a different mix, so you can compare them.

flow.do: Add one level teaspoon of dry yeast to A, B and C. Do not add yeast to D. Swirl each bottle for 10 seconds. Fit a stretched balloon on each bottle. Put C in the fridge on a low shelf. Leave A, B and D on a tray in the kitchen.
flow.say: Yeast goes into A, B and C, and not into D. Swirl each bottle. Now fit a balloon on the top of each one. The balloon will catch the gas.
flow.kid: Add one teaspoon of yeast to A, B and C. Do not add any to D. Swirl. Fit a balloon on each bottle. Put C in the fridge.
flow.parent: Dry yeast looks like tiny beige grains. Swirl gently so the bottle does not foam over. Leave nothing on top of bottle C in the fridge, so the balloon has room. Fit each balloon snugly over the neck, and add a rubber band if it is loose. If gas leaks out at the neck, the balloon stays flat even when the yeast are making gas. If your yeast sachet is old, first test a pinch in a cup of warm sugar water: it should foam in 10 minutes.
flow.context: In this step, you add the yeast and put on the balloons. The balloon will catch any gas the yeast make.

flow.do: Set a timer for 10 minutes. When it rings, wrap the tape measure around the widest part of each balloon. Write down each number. Take bottle C out of the fridge for the measuring, then put it back. Do this at 10, 20, 30 and 40 minutes.
flow.say: Set the timer for 10 minutes. When it rings, measure around the balloon on each bottle. Take C out of the fridge, measure it quickly, and put it back. Write the numbers in the table. Do it four times.
flow.kid: Set a timer for 10 minutes. Measure around each balloon. Write the numbers. Do this four times.

ask.q: What do you notice on the surface of the water in bottle A?

flow.parent: While you wait, read the card about yeast together. Bottle A usually starts to swell after about 15 to 20 minutes, and it keeps growing for about an hour. Sizes depend on your bottle, yeast and room, so do not worry if your numbers are small. If A is still tiny at 40 minutes, keep measuring at 50 and 60 minutes. If every balloon stays flat, check for a leaking neck, old yeast or water that was too hot, and say what you think happened. Bottle B may swell a little, because a little food may come in with the yeast sachet. That is also a result.

check.q: After 30 minutes, balloon A is much bigger than balloon D. What does this show?
options: Yeast are needed to make the gas
Sugar makes the balloon stretch
Warm water makes balloons bigger
check.why: Bottles A and D both have warm water and sugar. Only A has yeast. So the yeast made the gas.

flow.context: In this step, you watch and measure. The numbers show how much gas each bottle makes over 40 minutes.

flow.do: Draw a line graph with minutes along the bottom and balloon size up the side. Draw one line for each bottle. Then ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why. Pour the liquid down the sink and wash the bottles.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Draw a line for each bottle. Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.
flow.think: A baker wakes dry yeast with warm water and a little sugar. Why does that help?
flow.parent: A strong answer says that bottle A grew most because the yeast had sugar and warmth, and that D made no gas because it had no yeast. After they have said what they saw, explain: yeast eat sugar and make carbon dioxide gas. Cold slows them down. If B or C also swelled a little, say so. That is also a result.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Yeast Balloon test. You draw the graph and explain what you found.

experiments.title: The Curd Test: does milk need a starter, and does it need warmth?
experiments.question: Does boiled milk set into curd without a starter? And where does it set fastest: in a warm place, on the counter or in the fridge?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which cup will set first? Which will not set at all? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every cup has the same amount of the same milk, and the cups are the same kind. Cups A, B and C get the same amount of the same starter curd. They differ only in where they are kept: a warm place, the counter, or the fridge. Cup D gets no starter and is kept on the counter with B. Cup D is the control.

materials.item: 4 small steel cups or glasses, about 200 millilitres each, all the same
about 650 millilitres of milk, boiled by a grown-up and cooled until a clean finger can stay in it for 10 seconds
3 level teaspoons of fresh, plain curd as the starter (not sweet or flavoured, and not more than a day or two old)
4 clean teaspoons or spoons, and a marker or paper labels
4 small plates or lids to cover the cups
a warm place: a closed cupboard, or an oven with only its light switched on (it should feel pleasantly warm, not hot, on the hand)
the results table and a pencil

experiments.safety: A grown-up boils the milk and carries the hot pan. If you use the oven, put a note on the door so nobody switches on the heat. Do not use milk or curd if anyone in the family is allergic to dairy. Do not taste cup D, or any cup that smells bad or has colour on it. Taste only a small spoon from a cup that has set well.

schedule.what: Do this in the evening, around 8 or 9 pm. Guess first. Then boil and cool the milk. Fill the cups, add the starter to A, B and C, and put each cup in its place.
Morning check (7 minutes). Evening check and talk about the results (13 minutes).

experiments.record: Check each cup twice, once in the morning and once in the evening. Each time, give the cup a number from 0 (runny like milk) to 3 (firm), and write down how it smells.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you find out what milk needs to turn into curd. You change the starter and the temperature, one at a time.

setup.art: A grown-up pouring cooled milk from a steel pot into four equal steel cups labelled A, B, C and D, each filled to the same line.
setup.caption: 1. Pour the same amount of cooled milk into four cups.

setup.art: A teaspoon of curd being stirred into the milk in one cup, with a note that cup D gets no starter.
setup.caption: 2. Add one teaspoon of starter curd to A, B and C. Leave D without.

setup.art: Four cups covered with small plates: A in an oven with its light on, B and D on the kitchen counter, and C on a fridge shelf.
setup.caption: 3. Cover the cups and put each one in its place. Do not move them.

setup.art: A child gently tilting a cup to see if the curd is liquid, thick or firm, next to a scale from 0 to 3 with a drawing for each number.
setup.caption: 4. Tilt each cup gently. Give it a number from 0 to 3.

setup.art: A results table with four rows for cups A to D and a child writing numbers into it.
setup.caption: 5. Write the numbers in the table, and the smell.

flow.do: Show your child the four cups and say what goes in each. Write down their guess and their reason.
flow.say: We have four cups of milk. A, B and C each get a spoon of starter curd. D gets none. A goes in a warm place, B and D go on the counter, and C goes in the fridge. Which will set first? Which will not set at all? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Four cups of milk. A, B and C get starter curd. D does not. A is warm. B and D are on the counter. C is in the fridge. Which sets first? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think cup D will stay milk?
good: The milk has no bacteria added.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Roles: with one child, you boil the milk and your child fills the cups and writes the table. With 2 to 4 children, each child owns one cup (A, B, C or D) and its labels, spoon and number.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Curd Test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: A grown-up boils the milk, then lets it cool until a clean finger can stay in it for 10 seconds. Pour 150 millilitres into each of four cups. Label them A, B, C and D. Add one teaspoon of starter to A, B and C. Use a clean spoon each time. Stir gently. Do not add starter to D.
flow.say: The milk must be boiled first, then cooled to finger-warm. If it is too hot, it will kill the bacteria in the starter. Pour the same amount into each cup. Add a spoon of starter to A, B and C, and stir gently.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to boil the milk. Let it cool to finger-warm. Fill four cups. Add starter to A, B and C. Not D.
flow.parent: Too hot is worse than too cool. If the milk burns your finger, wait. Use a clean spoon for each cup so you do not carry starter into D.

check.q: Why must the milk cool before the starter goes in?
options: Hot milk would kill the bacteria in the starter
Hot milk would make the curd too sweet
Cool milk is easier to pour
check.why: Most bacteria begin to die above about 50 degrees Celsius. If the milk is too hot, the starter bacteria die and the milk will not set.

flow.context: In this step, you boil and cool the milk and add the starter. The starter carries the living bacteria.

flow.do: Cover each cup with a plate. Put A in the warm place. Put B and D on the counter. Put C on a shelf in the fridge. Do not stir or move the cups until morning.
flow.say: Each cup goes to its own place. A is warm, B and D are on the counter, and C is in the fridge. Please do not stir or move them. The bacteria need to be left alone.
flow.kid: Cover the cups. Put each cup in its place. Do not move them until morning.
flow.parent: After 10 minutes, put your hand in the warm place. It should feel pleasantly warm, not hot. If it feels hot, use a cupboard instead.
flow.context: In this step, you put the cups in their places. Then you wait for the bacteria to work.

flow.do: The next morning, about 10 hours later, slide the plate aside just enough to look into each cup. Tilt each one a little. Give each cup a number: 0 for runny like milk, 1 for slightly thick, 2 for set but soft, 3 for firm. Smell each cup. Write down the numbers.
flow.say: Tilt each cup gently, and see whether the top moves like milk or holds like a jelly. Give it a number from 0 to 3. Then smell it. What do you notice?
flow.kid: Tilt each cup gently. Give it a number from 0 to 3. Smell it. Write what you find.

ask.q: Which cups have changed, and which have stayed the same?
good: C and D are still milk.
Cup A is thicker than B.

flow.parent: In a hot kitchen, cups A and B may look alike, because both are warm enough. In a cool kitchen, A will be ahead. Write exactly what you see. In winter or in a cold kitchen, nothing may have set yet. That is a real result: keep checking until the next morning, and write down when each cup changed.
flow.context: In this step, you check the cups the next morning. You give each one a number to show how well it has set.

flow.do: In the evening, about 10 hours after the morning check, look at each cup again. Tilt each cup, give it a number from 0 to 3 and smell it. Write down the numbers. Taste a small spoonful only from a cup that has set well.
flow.say: Check the cups again. Which ones changed since the morning? Which stayed the same? Taste only a cup that has set well, and only a small spoon.
flow.kid: Check the cups again. Give each a number. Smell each one. Taste only a cup that has set well.
flow.parent: Cup C in the fridge may be thicker than in the morning, but is usually still runny. Cup D may smell slightly sour. That comes from other microbes that landed in it. Do not taste D.

check.q: Cup D had no starter. If cup D is still runny, what does this show?
options: Milk does not set into curd without the right bacteria
Milk never sets in the kitchen
Curd needs a plate on top
check.why: Cup B and cup D were kept in the same place. Only B had a starter, and only B set. So the starter was needed.

flow.context: In this step, you check the cups again in the evening and compare them with the morning.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why. Then sort the cups from the firmest to the runniest, and write which thing mattered more, the starter or the warmth.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened? Which mattered more, the starter or the warmth?
flow.kid: Say what you thought, what you saw, and why. Which mattered more, the starter or the warmth?
flow.think: How could you make curd in a very cold winter kitchen?
flow.parent: A strong answer says that the starter was needed, because D did not set. Warmth made it faster, because A and B set before C. After they have said what they saw, explain: the bacteria in the starter eat milk sugar and make lactic acid. The acid makes the milk protein join into a net. Cold slows the bacteria down.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Curd Test. You explain what you found.

activities.title: Batter Watch: one bowl, one night

materials.item: about 2 cups of fresh idli or dosa batter, ground that day
a tall clear jar or a steel container, about 1 litre
a second jar like the first, and a plate or lid to cover each jar loosely (optional: for the fridge comparison)
a rubber band or a marker pen
a ruler
paper and a pencil

activities.safety: Do not eat batter that smells bad or has pink, green or black colour on it. Do not taste the raw batter.

schedule.what: Pour the batter into the jar. Mark the level. Guess how high it will be in the morning.
Measure the rise. Smell, listen and look. Draw the batter. Say why it changed.

activities.record: Write the height of the batter at the start and in the morning. Draw the inside of the jar, with bubbles.
activities.context: In this activity, you watch a jar of batter overnight. You measure how far it rises, and look, smell and listen for signs of microbes at work.

setup.art: A tall clear jar half filled with smooth batter, with a rubber band marking the level and a ruler beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Pour batter into a jar. Mark the level with a rubber band.

setup.art: The same jar in the morning, with the batter risen above the rubber band and tiny bubbles on the top and sides.
setup.caption: 2. Next morning, look at the batter. Measure how high it rose.

setup.art: A child with an ear close to the jar, eyes closed, and a nose close to the top.
setup.caption: 3. Listen. Smell. What do you notice?

flow.do: Pour the batter into the jar until it is one third full. Slip a rubber band around the jar at the top of the batter. Measure the height with a ruler. Write the number down. Cover the jar loosely with a plate. If you have a second jar, fill it the same way and put it in the fridge. Ask your child for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: We will leave the batter overnight. How high do you think it will be in the morning? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Pour batter into the jar. Mark the top with a rubber band. Measure it. How high will it be tomorrow? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the batter will rise?
good: Tiny living things in it make gas.
Gas gets trapped in the batter.

flow.parent: A third full leaves room to rise. Cover loosely, never tight, so the gas can escape. Keep the jar in a warm part of the kitchen, away from the fan. If your kitchen is cold, the batter may not rise much. That is also a result. With 2 to 4 children, each child can set up and measure their own jar: one on the counter, one in the fridge.
flow.context: This is the first step of Batter Watch. You mark the height and guess what will happen.

flow.do: The next morning, look at the jar. Measure how high the batter is now. Write down the number. Look at the bubbles. Smell the top. Hold your ear close, and listen. Draw the inside of the jar, with the bubbles. If you have the fridge jar, measure it too and compare.
flow.say: What do you see? What do you smell? What do you hear? How high did it rise? Why do you think it rose?
flow.kid: Measure the batter. Look at the bubbles. Smell it. Listen. Draw what you see.

ask.q: What do the bubbles tell you?

flow.think: What would the batter look like if you had left it in the fridge?
flow.parent: Fresh-ground batter in a warm kitchen usually rises well overnight; the fridge jar hardly rises. In hot weather it may rise a lot and smell quite sour, which is fine. A good rise is about one and a half times the starting height or more, with bubbles through the batter and a slightly sour smell. If it did not rise, check the room temperature and try the Winter Batter challenge. After they have shared what they saw, explain: the microbes ate the sugars and made carbon dioxide, and the sticky dal held the gas.

check.q: A jar of batter rose in the night and smells a little sour. What made the sour smell?
options: Bacteria making lactic acid
Salt in the batter
The jar
check.why: Bacteria in the batter eat sugar and make lactic acid. That is the same acid that makes curd sour.

flow.context: This is the last step of Batter Watch. You measure, smell, listen and draw.

activities.title: Ask the Elders: the fermented foods of our family

materials.item: a notebook page with a 5-column table
a pencil
a phone, to call a grandparent or an older relative, or to ask a grown-up at home
a rough outline of India drawn by hand, or the printed map in your atlas

schedule.what: Interview an elder or a grown-up about fermented foods. Fill in the table. Mark the foods on a map.

activities.record: A table with at least five foods: the food, what it is made from, who makes it, how long it takes, and how you know it is ready.
activities.context: In this activity, you collect the fermented foods that your family or your region knows. You also ask how they know when each one is ready.

setup.art: A girl holding a phone on speaker, writing in a notebook while her grandmother talks on the other end.
setup.caption: 1. Ask an elder which foods they make with fermenting.

setup.art: A notebook table with columns: Food, Made from, Who makes it, How long, How you know it is ready.
setup.caption: 2. Fill in the table for each food.

setup.art: A hand-drawn outline of India with small drawings of foods placed in different regions.
setup.caption: 3. Mark each food on a map of India.

flow.do: Draw a table with five columns: Food, Made from, Who makes it, How long it takes, How you know it is ready.
flow.say: Our elders know a lot about fermented foods. Let's collect what they know, like scientists collecting information.
flow.kid: Draw a table with five columns. You will interview someone who knows about food.
flow.context: This is the first step of Ask the Elders. You get your table ready.

flow.do: Call a grandparent or an older relative, or ask a grown-up at home. Ask them to name foods that sit and change before they are eaten, such as curd, batter, pickle or bread. Fill in the table. Ask them to tell one story about how they learned to make it.
flow.say: Which foods do you make that have to be left for a day or more to change? What are they made from? How do you know when they are ready?
flow.kid: Ask your elder which foods they leave to change before eating. Ask how they know it is ready. Write it down.

ask.q: How do you know when it is ready?

flow.parent: If nobody in the family makes fermented food, ask a neighbour or a shop owner. Idli, dosa, curd, pickle, bread, vinegar and kanji all count. People often know a food is ready by smell, sight and taste. With one child, you can ask and your child writes. With 2 to 4 children, one asks, one writes and one draws the map; each child can interview a different elder. Elders are glad to tell the stories behind a food.
flow.context: In this step, you interview someone. You write down the foods, and how the person knows each one is ready.

flow.do: Look at the foods in your table. Decide, for each one, whether you think bacteria, yeast or mould does the work. Write your guess in a new column.
flow.say: Which microbe do you think does the work in each food? Remember, bacteria make acid and yeast make gas. Make your best guess.
flow.kid: For each food, guess the microbe. Bacteria make acid. Yeast make gas. Write your guess.
flow.parent: Many foods have both bacteria and yeast. Curd and buttermilk are mostly bacteria. Bread, appam and toddy are mostly yeast. Idli batter has both. Any sensible guess is fine.
flow.context: In this step, you guess which microbe does the work in each food.

flow.do: Draw a rough outline of India. Mark where each food comes from, and draw a tiny picture of it. Look for foods from three different parts of India.
flow.say: Where in India is each food from? Are they all from the same region? Why might different places make different foods?
flow.kid: Draw India. Mark where each food comes from. Draw a tiny picture of it.
flow.think: Why do you think different places in India have different fermented foods?
flow.parent: People use what grows near them: rice and dal in the south, gram flour in Gujarat, black carrots in Punjab and soybeans in the north-east. Look at the card on fermented foods across India for ideas.
flow.context: This is the last step of Ask the Elders. You place the foods on a map.

activities.title: Kitchen Safari: which foods were made with microbes?

materials.item: a pencil and a sheet of paper
the kitchen, the fridge and the food shelf
a grown-up to open the fridge and read labels with you

schedule.what: Walk through the kitchen. Find foods that were made with microbes. Check the labels. Sort them.

activities.record: A list of at least eight foods, sorted into two groups: made with microbes, and not made with microbes, with a count for each group and a note on how your first guess compared.
activities.context: In this activity, you search your kitchen for foods that were made with the help of microbes. You check labels and sort them.

setup.art: A child opening a fridge door and pointing at a pot of curd, a packet of paneer and a jar of pickle.
setup.caption: 1. Look in the fridge and the food shelf.

setup.art: A close-up of a food packet showing the words yeast, culture or starter on the ingredients list.
setup.caption: 2. Read the label. Look for yeast, culture or starter.

setup.art: A sheet of paper divided into two columns, one for made with microbes and one for not.
setup.caption: 3. Sort your foods into two groups.

flow.do: Walk through the kitchen with your child. First, ask your child to guess how many of the foods you will see were made with microbes. Then find at least eight foods that you think were made with microbes. Write down the names.
flow.say: Let's look for foods that microbes helped to make. Curd and bread are easy. What else can you find?
flow.kid: Look around the kitchen. Find foods you think microbes helped make. Write them down.
flow.parent: Easy finds: curd, buttermilk, bread, idli or dosa batter, cheese, soy sauce, and some pickles, which are fermented in salt. Tricky ones: oil-and-spice pickles are only preserved, and some cheap vinegar and soy sauce are made with chemicals, so the label decides. Ketchup is not fermented, but its vinegar is made by microbes. Papad is not fermented. Foods that are not made with microbes: rice, plain milk, paneer, dal, fresh vegetables, sugar. With 2 to 4 children, each takes a shelf and then they compare. A grown-up opens the fridge and handles glass jars and knives.
flow.context: This is the first step of Kitchen Safari. You search the kitchen.

flow.do: Pick up three packets. Read the labels together. Look for the words yeast, culture, starter or fermented. Write down which words you find.
flow.say: Many labels tell you if microbes were used. Look for the words yeast, culture, starter or fermented. What do you find?
flow.kid: Read the label. Look for yeast, culture, starter or fermented. Write what you find.

check.q: Which of these is not made by microbes?
options: Paneer, made by adding lemon juice or vinegar to hot milk
Curd
Bread
check.why: Paneer is made by adding an acid to hot milk, so that the milk protein clumps together. No microbes are needed. Curd and bread both need living microbes.

flow.context: In this step, you read labels to see which foods say they were made with microbes.

flow.do: Draw two columns on a sheet. Write Made with microbes on one side and Not made with microbes on the other. Sort your foods. Count each column and compare with your first guess. Talk about the ones you are not sure about.
flow.say: Which column does each food go in? Which ones are you not sure about? How could you find out?
flow.kid: Sort your foods into two columns. Which ones are you not sure about?
flow.think: How could you find out whether a food was made with microbes?
flow.context: This is the last step of Kitchen Safari. You sort the foods.

projects.title: Make idli from scratch: from rice and dal to soft idli

materials.item: 1 cup of idli rice, or parboiled rice
one third of a cup of whole or split urad dal, without skin
half a teaspoon of fenugreek seeds (methi), if you have them
1 teaspoon of salt, and a little oil for greasing the idli plates
a mixer or a wet grinder (a grown-up uses it)
a large steel pot with a loose lid, big enough for the batter to double
an idli steamer, or a pressure cooker with idli plates and no weight on the lid
a rubber band and a ruler, to mark the level of the batter

projects.safety: A grown-up works the grinder, because the blades are sharp. A grown-up does the steaming. The steam and the pot are very hot. Children stay back when the lid is opened. Nobody tastes the raw batter.

schedule.what: Wash and soak the rice and the dal. Four to five hours later, a grown-up grinds them. Mix, add salt and set the batter in a warm place for the night.
Check the batter. Steam the idlis with a grown-up. Taste them, and compare with idli you have eaten before.

projects.record: Write the height of the batter before and after the night, how it smelled, and how your idlis turned out. Draw an idli cut in half.
projects.context: In this project, you make idli yourself, from soaked rice and dal. You watch microbes make the batter rise, and then you steam and taste the result.

setup.art: A bowl of idli rice and a bowl of urad dal, each covered with water on a kitchen counter.
setup.caption: 1. Wash and soak the rice and the dal in separate bowls.

setup.art: A grown-up grinding soaked dal into a light, fluffy batter in a mixer jar.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up grinds the dal until it is fluffy, then the rice until it is a little rough.

setup.art: A steel pot with a rubber band marking the batter level, and a loose lid, standing in a warm corner of the kitchen.
setup.caption: 3. Mix, add salt, mark the level, cover loosely and leave overnight.

setup.art: A grown-up filling idli plates with risen batter and placing them in a steamer.
setup.caption: 4. Next morning, steam the idlis for 10 to 12 minutes.

flow.do: Wash one cup of rice and the dal separately, until the water runs almost clear. Soak the rice in one bowl, and the dal with the fenugreek seeds in a different bowl. Cover both with water. Leave them for 4 to 5 hours.
flow.say: Rice and dal soak separately. Soaking softens them so they grind smoothly. It also wakes up the microbes that live on the grains. Which microbe do you think will do the work?
flow.kid: Wash the rice and the dal. Soak them in two bowls. Wait 4 to 5 hours.

ask.q: Why do you think we soak the rice and dal before grinding?
good: To get them ready for the microbes.

flow.parent: Use cool water. While the rice and dal soak, you can do other lessons. The grains are already covered with microbes that will wake up in the batter. Roles: with one child, your child washes and soaks while you grind and steam. With 2 to 4 children, one washes the rice, one the dal, one marks and measures the batter, and one greases the plates (a grown-up fills them).
flow.context: This is the first step of Make Idli. You soak the rice and the dal.

flow.do: A grown-up pours off the water, keeping a little. The grown-up grinds the dal until it is light and fluffy. Then the grown-up grinds the rice until it is slightly rough. Mix the two batters in the pot.
flow.say: Grinding the dal until it is light and fluffy gives the batter its stickiness. That stickiness will hold the gas later. The rice batter is slightly rough, like fine sand.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to grind the dal and the rice. Watch the batter get light and fluffy.
flow.parent: Add water a little at a time. The dal batter should look like thick cream. Mix the rice and the dal with clean, dry hands or a clean ladle.
flow.context: In this step, a grown-up grinds the soaked rice and dal. Then you mix the batter.

flow.do: Stir in one teaspoon of salt. Pour the batter into the big pot so that it is no more than one third full. Slip a rubber band around the pot at the top of the batter. Measure the height. Cover the pot loosely. Put it in a warm place overnight.
flow.say: The pot must be big, so the batter has room to rise. Mark the level, so we can see how much it rises. The lid must be loose, so the gas can escape.
flow.kid: Add salt. Pour the batter into the pot. Mark the top with a rubber band. Cover it loosely. Leave it overnight.
flow.parent: In a cool kitchen, below about 22 degrees, use a warm cupboard or the oven with only its light on. See the Winter Batter challenge. Leave a note on the oven door so nobody switches on the heat. Write down the starting height. Batter usually needs 8 to 12 hours at 25 to 30 degrees; in hot weather it can be ready sooner and quite sour.

check.q: Why must the lid on the pot stay loose?
options: The microbes make gas, and it needs to escape
The batter needs air from outside
To keep the batter warm
check.why: The microbes make carbon dioxide all night. A tight lid can build up pressure and burst.

flow.context: In this step, you mix the batter, mark its level and leave it for the microbes to work.

flow.do: The next morning, measure the height of the batter. Smell it. Look at the bubbles. Write down the numbers. Do not stir it hard.
flow.say: Has it risen? How much higher is it now? What does it smell like? Why do you think it rose?
flow.kid: Measure the batter. Smell it. Look at the bubbles. How much did it rise?

good: Gas got trapped in the sticky batter.
The bacteria and yeast ate sugar.

flow.parent: A good rise is one and a half to two times the starting height, with bubbles and a pleasant sour smell. If it has not risen, say so, and wait 3 to 4 more hours in a warm place, or try the Winter Batter challenge. If it still has not risen, steam it anyway: the idlis will be flat but safe to eat. Throw the batter away if it smells bad or has colour on it. After they have shared what they saw, explain: microbes ate the sugars and made carbon dioxide gas.
flow.context: In this step, you check how much the batter has risen overnight.

flow.do: A grown-up greases the idli plates and fills each cup with batter. The grown-up steams them for 10 to 12 minutes. Wait for 5 minutes before taking them out.
flow.say: Steam is very hot, so only a grown-up opens the steamer. The heat kills the microbes. It also sets the sticky batter, with all the tiny gas bubbles inside.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to fill the plates and steam the idlis. Wait until they are cool enough to touch.
flow.parent: An idli is done when a clean spoon comes out dry. Let it cool for a few minutes so it does not break.
flow.context: In this step, a grown-up steams the idlis. The heat kills the microbes and sets the batter.

flow.do: Cut an idli in half. Look at the holes inside. Draw what you see. Taste it with a chutney or sambar. Say what you think made the holes.
flow.say: Look at the holes inside the idli. What made them? Where did the gas go? How is it different from an idli you have had before?
flow.kid: Cut an idli in half. Draw the holes. Taste it. What made the holes?
flow.think: How would you change the recipe to make the idlis softer?
flow.parent: The holes were made by gas bubbles that the microbes made. The sticky dal held them in place, and the steam set them. If your idlis are flat, the batter may have been too cold or too thin. Try again with the Winter Batter ideas.
flow.context: This is the last step of Make Idli. You cut an idli open, look inside and taste it.

challenges.title: Winter Batter: keep the batter warm in a cold kitchen
challenges.problem: It is winter, and your kitchen is cold. To rise, the batter needs to stay about as warm as a spring day for 10 hours. Design a way to keep a pot warm without a flame, using only things you find at home.
constraints: Use only things you have at home.
Never leave a flame or a hot stove on.
The pot must not get too hot to touch comfortably.
The lid must stay loose so the gas can escape.
You must test your design and measure what happens.
materials: a steel pot with a loose lid
3 clean bottles filled with the same amount of warm water
towels, a woollen shawl or a blanket
a cardboard box or a lunch box
an oven with a light, if you have one
a thermometer, if you have one
general: Wrap the pot in a thick towel, then put it in a box. Put a bottle of warm water beside it.
Put the pot in an oven with only the light on. Leave a note on the door.
Put the pot in a closed cupboard near a warm place, such as above the fridge, where the back of the fridge gives off a little heat.
creative: Put the pot inside a larger bucket with a few bottles of warm water around it, and wrap the bucket in a blanket. Use a pot with a lid that is not tight.
Use a thermocol box from a delivery as a small oven, with a bottle of warm water inside.
Stir in a spoonful of yesterday's batter. The microbes in it are already active, so they will begin quickly even in a cooler place.
challenges.your_turn: Test two ways to keep a bottle of warm water warm. Check each bottle after 3 hours with your finger or a thermometer. Pick the best way. Then try it with a pot of batter overnight and check the batter in the morning.
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about microbes and warmth. You keep a pot of batter warm in a cold kitchen, without a flame.

setup.art: Three identical bottles of warm water: one bare, one wrapped in a towel, and one wrapped in a towel inside a box.
setup.caption: 1. Test three ways of keeping a bottle of warm water warm.

setup.art: A child touching each bottle after three hours, with a thermometer beside it.
setup.caption: 2. After three hours, check which bottle is still warm.

setup.art: A steel pot of batter wrapped in a towel inside a cardboard box, with a warm bottle beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Use the best way to keep a pot of batter warm overnight.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Talk about why cold batter does not rise. Ask for ideas for keeping something warm.
flow.say: Cold makes the microbes slow. How could you keep a pot warm, without a flame, using things at home?
flow.kid: Cold batter does not rise. How could you keep it warm? Think of ideas.

ask.q: What keeps you warm in winter?

flow.context: This is the first step of Winter Batter. You think about the problem.

flow.do: Fill three identical bottles with the same warm water. Leave one bare. Wrap one in a towel. Wrap one in a towel and put it in a box. Leave them for 3 hours. Then feel each one, or measure it with a thermometer.
flow.say: We are testing three ways to keep something warm. Which will stay warm the longest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Fill three bottles with warm water. Wrap them in different ways. Check them in 3 hours.
flow.parent: The warm water should feel comfortable on your wrist, not hot. The bottle wrapped in a towel inside the box will usually stay warmest, because wrapping slows the escape of heat.
flow.context: In this step, you test three ways of keeping a bottle of water warm.

flow.do: Pick your best way. Draw your design, and say why you chose it. Add one idea of your own.
flow.say: Which way kept the water warmest? How could you make it even better? What is your own idea?
flow.kid: Choose the best way. Draw it. Add your own idea.
flow.context: In this step, you pick your best design and add your own idea.

flow.do: Put a pot of fresh batter into your design. Mark the level with a rubber band. In the morning, check how high it has risen, and how it smells.
flow.say: Did it work? How high did the batter rise? What would you do differently next time?
flow.kid: Put a pot of batter in your design. Mark the level. Check it in the morning.
flow.think: What would you change in your design to make it work even better?
flow.parent: If the batter did not rise, try again with a spoonful of yesterday's batter stirred in, or with a warmer place. A result that did not work is still a result.
flow.context: This is the last step of Winter Batter. You test your design with real batter.

items.p: Which three things do microbes need to grow well?
opts: Food, water and the right warmth
items.why: Microbes are living beings. Like you, they need food and water. Most helpful ones in the kitchen grow best in gentle warmth. Cold slows them, and too much heat kills them.

items.p: Yeast is a kind of what?
opts: A fungus with one round cell
items.why: Yeast belongs to the fungi, the same group as mushrooms and moulds. A yeast cell is a single round cell. Bacteria are a different group.

items.p: The bubbles in rising bread dough are carbon dioxide gas made by yeast.
items.why: True. Yeast eat sugar and make carbon dioxide. The stretchy dough traps the gas in tiny bubbles, and the dough rises.

items.p: The sour taste of curd comes from ____ acid.
items.why: Bacteria in the curd eat the sugar in milk and make lactic acid. That acid is what makes curd sour and thick.

items.p: Match each food to what the microbes in it make.
pairs: gas and acid, made by bacteria and yeast
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Different microbes make different things from sugar. Bacteria in curd make acid. Yeast in dough make gas. Yeast in palm sap make alcohol. Idli batter has both bacteria and yeast.

items.p: Why does a spoon of old curd turn a pot of warm milk into curd?
opts: It carries living bacteria that eat the milk sugar
It adds extra sugar to the milk
items.why: The spoon carries millions of living bacteria. In warm milk they eat the milk sugar, make lactic acid and multiply. The acid makes the milk set.

items.p: Sort each situation by what it does to yeast.
items.a: as given
items.why: Yeast grow best in gentle warmth with food. Cold slows them. Heat above about 60 degrees kills them.

items.p: A fridge kills the microbes in food.
items.why: False. A fridge slows microbes down, but most stay alive. That is why food in the fridge still spoils in time.

items.p: A balloon on a bottle of yeast and sugar water measures 4 centimetres around at 10 minutes, 10 at 20 minutes and 16 at 30 minutes. How many centimetres did it grow between 10 and 30 minutes?
items.why: 16 take away 4 is 12. The balloon grew by 12 centimetres, because the yeast kept making gas.

items.p: A friend says: 'Idli batter rises because I grind it very well.' What would you tell your friend, using what you know about microbes?
items.a: Grinding makes the batter smooth and sticky, which helps hold gas. But the rise comes from microbes in the batter that eat sugar and make gas. If the batter is kept cold, it will not rise even if it was ground well.
items.why: A strong answer says that living microbes make the gas, and that the batter needs warmth for them to work. It may also say that grinding helps trap the gas.

items.p: Which of these is spoiled food, and not fermented food?
items.why: Fuzzy patches are mould, which means unwanted microbes have grown. Sour curd and bubbly batter are changed by helpful microbes that we want.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? Curd, idli batter, bread dough, paneer.
items.a: Paneer, because it is made by adding acid to hot milk. The other three are made by living microbes.
items.why: Paneer is made when an acid, such as lemon juice, makes the milk protein clump together. No microbes are needed.

items.p: A spoonful of old curd used to begin a new batch is called a ____.
items.why: It is called a starter because it starts the next batch, with bacteria that are already alive.

items.p: Draw a yeast cell with a small bud. Then draw a piece of dough with bubbles of carbon dioxide inside.
items.a: A round cell with a smaller round bump growing from it, and a piece of dough with several round bubbles inside.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the bud still attached to the first cell, and the bubbles held inside the dough, not floating outside it.

items.p: Dry yeast in a packet is dormant. What does that mean?
items.why: Dormant means alive but almost inactive. Warm water and sugar wake the yeast up. That is why they begin to foam.

items.p: Curd that has not been heated after it has set holds living bacteria.
items.why: True. The bacteria that made the curd are still alive in the curd, though they work slowly once the curd is cold.

items.p: In winter, idli batter takes much longer to rise than in summer. Explain why.
items.a: The microbes grow slowly when it is cold. Warmth makes them eat and make gas faster, so in a cold kitchen the batter takes longer to rise.
items.why: A strong answer says that cold slows the microbes down, and that the gas they make is what makes the batter rise.

items.p: Why does the gluten in wheat dough matter for bread?
opts: It stretches into a net that traps the gas
items.why: Gluten is a stretchy protein. When you knead flour and water, it forms a net. The gas pushes against the net and stretches it, and the dough rises.

items.p: Two batters have microbes that make the same amount of gas. Batter X is rice and dal. Batter Y is rice only. Batter X rises much more. Why?
opts: The sticky dal batter holds the gas in
Rice has no sugar in it
items.why: The gas has to be held in or it escapes. Dal makes the batter thick and sticky, so it traps the gas. Rice batter alone is thin, and the gas bubbles out.

items.p: A packet of dry yeast that has been open for a year in a hot cupboard should be tested before baking.
items.why: True. Heat and age can kill many yeast cells. A baker tests a pinch in warm sugar water. If it foams, the yeast are alive.

items.p: Heating milk to kill harmful microbes, without cooking it, is called ____.
items.why: The word pasteurising comes from Louis Pasteur, who showed that gentle heat can kill the microbes that spoil food.

items.p: Match each microbe to the job they do.
pairs: help break down fibre in food
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Microbes do many useful jobs. Some make food, some make medicine, some clean up dead plants, and some live in our bodies and help digest.

items.p: Yeast in warm dough double in number every 90 minutes. You start with 1 cell. How many cells are there after 6 hours?
items.why: 6 hours is 360 minutes. 360 divided by 90 is 4 doublings. 1 doubled four times is 2, 4, 8, 16. So there are 16 cells.

items.p: A friend says: 'I can cut the mould off the bread and eat the rest.' What would you tell your friend, and why?
items.a: Do not eat it. Mould sends thin threads deep into soft bread, even where you cannot see them. Some moulds make poisons. Throw the whole piece away.
items.why: A strong answer says that mould spreads inside soft food where you cannot see it, and that the whole piece should be thrown away.

items.p: Sort each food: was it made with the help of microbes, or not?
items.a: as given
items.why: Curd, dosa batter, vinegar and pav need living microbes. Paneer is made with acid. Plain milk, rice and sugar are not changed by microbes.

items.p: Put these in the right order, for how idli is made.
a: Rice and dal are ground into a sticky batter
Microbes on the grains eat the sugars
The microbes make carbon dioxide gas and lactic acid
The sticky batter traps the gas and rises
Steam kills the microbes and sets the idli
items.why: The microbes must make the gas before the batter can rise. Steaming comes last, because the heat stops the microbes and sets the idli.

items.p: Dry yeast is stirred into boiling water, and sugar is added. No bubbles appear. What is the best explanation?
items.why: Yeast die in water hotter than about 50 degrees. Dead yeast cannot eat sugar or make gas.

items.p: Which one is not made by microbes eating sugar? Carbon dioxide, lactic acid, alcohol, iron.
items.a: Iron. The other three are made when microbes ferment sugar.
items.why: Iron is a metal, an element. Microbes can make gas, acid and alcohol from sugar, but they cannot make an element.

items.p: A company sells a drink and says its bacteria will make your gut perfectly healthy.

views.says: Our drink holds millions of living bacteria. Many customers tell us they feel better after drinking it.
Gut bacteria matter, but the science is young. One drink is not enough to claim a perfectly healthy gut. We need careful tests.
I would rather spend on a varied meal with vegetables, dal and curd than on an expensive drink.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with most? What evidence would help you decide?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a view, gives a reason, and says what test or evidence would help, such as comparing groups of people who drink it and who do not.
items.why: This question has no single right answer. A strong answer shows that the child can weigh a claim, and asks for evidence.

items.p: Curd and pickle often stay safe longer than fresh milk or fresh vegetables kept in the same place. Why?
opts: The helpful microbes make acid that stops harmful microbes growing
They are thicker, so microbes cannot move
items.why: Acid makes it hard for many harmful microbes to grow. This is one reason people have used fermenting to keep food for longer.

items.p: Draw a bowl of curd with a spoon. Then draw a circle zoomed in on one drop, showing bacteria turning milk sugar into lactic acid.
items.a: A bowl of curd with a spoon, and a zoomed circle with small rod-shaped bacteria and arrows from a sugar to an acid.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the bacteria and shows the change, from sugar into acid. The bacteria appear only in the zoomed circle, because they are too small to see in the bowl.

items.p: Carbon dioxide gas is made when yeast eat ____.
items.why: Yeast need food. They eat sugar and make carbon dioxide and a little alcohol.

items.p: Antibiotics such as penicillin work against colds and flu.
items.why: False. Antibiotics work against bacteria. Colds and flu are caused by viruses, which antibiotics do not stop.

items.p: A pot holds one litre of milk, and you add only one spoon of old curd. Explain how one spoon can turn the whole pot into curd.
items.a: The spoon carries living bacteria. In warm milk they eat the milk sugar and split into two again and again. In a few hours there are many millions of bacteria. They make enough lactic acid to set the whole pot.
items.why: A strong answer says that bacteria multiply, and that the acid they make is what sets the milk. A spoon is enough because the bacteria make more of themselves.

items.p: A bacterium in warm milk splits into two every 30 minutes. Start with 1. How many bacteria are there after 4 hours?
items.why: 4 hours is 8 periods of 30 minutes. The number doubles each time: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256. So there are 256 bacteria.

items.p: Some cups of milk are set up. Cup P has starter and is kept warm. Cup Q has starter and is kept in the fridge. Cup R has no starter and is kept warm. After 10 hours only P has set. What does this best show?
opts: Both a starter and warmth are needed
items.why: Cup P has both and set. Cup Q has the starter but is cold, and did not set. Cup R is warm but has no starter, and did not set. So both are needed.

items.p: A new idli factory has to decide how to start its batter.

views.who: A grandmother in Mysuru (an imagined view)
views.says: I always stir in a spoon of yesterday's batter. It carries the right microbes for our home, and it is free.
In a factory we need the same idli every day. I would use a tested mix of microbes in measured amounts, so each batch is safe and the same.

items.ask: Which way would you choose for a big factory, and which for your own kitchen? Why might the two answers be different?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer sees that a factory needs safe and steady results at a large scale, and that a home can use a traditional starter that works well enough.
items.why: Both views have real strengths. A strong answer gives a reason for each choice, and says what the factory or the home needs most.

items.p: It is winter and your batter will not rise. Give two different things you could try, and explain why each one should work.
items.a: Keep the pot in a warm place, such as an oven with only its light on, because microbes work faster when warm. Stir in a spoon of yesterday's batter, because it brings microbes that are already active.
items.why: A strong answer gives two different ideas and links each to what microbes need, such as warmth, or an active starter.

items.p: Which test would be fair for finding out whether sugar changes how fast yeast make gas?
opts: Two bottles with the same water, the same warmth and the same yeast, with sugar in only one
One warm bottle with sugar and one cold bottle without sugar
One bottle with yeast and sugar, and one with only sugar
items.why: In a fair test only one thing changes. The first choice changes only the sugar. The second changes both warmth and sugar. The third changes the yeast and the sugar.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? Yeast, Penicillium, Leuconostoc, a mushroom.
items.a: Leuconostoc, because it is a bacterium. The other three are fungi.
items.why: Yeast, Penicillium moulds and mushrooms are all fungi. Leuconostoc is a bacterium that helps ferment idli batter.

items.p: Heating the batter in the steamer is what makes the batter ferment.
items.why: False. Fermenting happens earlier, when the microbes are alive and warm. Steam kills the microbes and sets the batter, so fermenting stops.

items.p: The stretchy protein net in wheat dough that traps gas is called ____.
items.why: Gluten forms when flour and water are kneaded. It makes dough stretchy, so it can hold the gas that the yeast make.

items.p: Before Pasteur, many scientists thought that fermentation did not need living things. Describe a simple test that could show whether living microbes are needed.
items.a: Take two flasks of sugar broth. Boil one to kill any microbes and keep it sealed. Leave the other untreated. If only the untreated flask ferments, then living microbes are needed.
items.why: A strong answer kills the microbes in one sample and compares it with another that is the same in every other way. It uses a control, as in a fair test.

items.p: Match what you see to what it most likely means.
pairs: Bubbles and a sour smell in batter
Fuzzy green patches on a chapati
mould, so throw the chapati away
Foam and a bread smell in yeast and sugar water
Curd still runny in a cold kitchen
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Signs tell us what microbes are doing. Gas and acid mean helpful microbes are working. Fuzzy mould means spoilage. Cold slows bacteria down.

items.p: Draw how one spoon of starter curd passes from an old pot of curd into a new pot of milk, and show what happens to the bacteria over the night.
items.a: An old pot with a spoon, an arrow to a new pot of milk, and bacteria drawn few at the start and many at the end.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that the bacteria are carried by the spoon, and that there are more of them in the morning because they have been splitting.

items.p: Sort each food by which microbe mainly does the work.
items.a: as given
items.why: Curd and buttermilk are made by bacteria. Bread, toddy and risen appam batter are made by yeast. Penicillin is made by a mould.

items.p: When someone says 'I made the curd', which is the best description of what the cook really did?
opts: Made a warm, sweet place where the bacteria could do the work
Turned the milk into acid by stirring
items.why: The cook boiled and cooled the milk and added the starter. The bacteria did the changing.

items.p: Every microbe found in a fermented food is harmless to people.
items.why: False. Fermented food is safe because the microbes we want make acid that keeps harmful ones away. But food that is spoiled can hold harmful microbes, so it must be thrown away.

items.p: Two kitchens make idli batter in the same way, but the batters have slightly different microbes. What is the most likely reason?
opts: The microbes come from the grains, utensils and air of each kitchen
Microbes come only from the salt
The two kitchens use different kinds of steam
items.why: Most home-made batter is not given microbes on purpose. They arrive on the rice, the dal, the grinder and the air. Every kitchen has its own mix.

items.p: A dosa batter recipe uses 4 cups of rice for every 1 cup of dal. You want to use 3 cups of dal. How many cups of rice do you need?
items.why: The recipe keeps the same ratio of 4 rice to 1 dal. 3 cups of dal is 3 times 1 cup, so you need 3 times 4 cups of rice. 3 times 4 is 12.

opts: Microbes eat sugar and make gas, acid or alcohol
Food is cooked until it turns sour
quiz.why: Fermentation is done by living microbes. They eat sugars and change them into new things, such as gas, acid or alcohol.

quiz.p: Which gas fills a balloon on a bottle of yeast, sugar and warm water?
quiz.why: Yeast eat sugar and make carbon dioxide. Steam would need boiling water, and the water is only warm.

quiz.p: Which substance makes curd taste sour?
quiz.why: Lactic acid bacteria make lactic acid from milk sugar. The acid makes the milk sour and thick.

quiz.p: What makes the dough rise when a baker uses yeast?
opts: Gas made by the yeast, trapped in the dough
quiz.why: Yeast make carbon dioxide as they eat. The stretchy dough holds the gas, and the whole dough rises.

quiz.p: A child wants to test whether salt slows yeast. Which bottle is the control?
opts: The bottle with yeast, sugar and warm water but no salt
The bottle with the most salt
quiz.why: The control has everything except the thing you are testing. It shows what happens anyway, so you can compare.

quiz.p: On a line graph of balloon size over time, what would the line for a bottle with no yeast most likely look like?
quiz.why: Without yeast, nothing makes gas. The balloon stays flat, so the line stays flat along the bottom.

quiz.p: Milk has just boiled and is very hot. What happens if you stir in the starter curd now?
opts: The bacteria in the starter die, and the milk does not set
quiz.why: Heat above about 50 degrees kills most bacteria. The starter only works if the milk is cooled to finger-warm first.

quiz.p: At which temperature would the bacteria that make curd work fastest?
quiz.why: They grow best in gentle warmth. At 5 degrees they are slow, and at 80 degrees they die.

quiz.p: You find a pot of curd with pink patches on top and a bad smell. What should you do?
opts: Scoop out the patches and eat the rest
quiz.why: Coloured patches and a bad smell are signs of spoilage. Unwanted microbes have grown, and the curd may make you ill.

quiz.p: Which smell is a normal sign that idli batter has fermented well?
opts: A mild sour smell with many small bubbles
quiz.why: Lactic acid gives a mild sour smell, and the gas makes bubbles. Rotten smells mean spoilage. No bubbles means nothing has happened yet.

quiz.p: What do fungi and bacteria in soil do with fallen leaves?
opts: Break them down into simple parts that plants can use again
quiz.why: These microbes are decomposers. They break down dead leaves, and the simple parts go back into the soil for new plants to use.

quiz.p: In Pasteur's curved-neck flask, the boiled broth stayed clear. Why?
opts: Microbes in the air could not reach the broth
Boiling made the broth too sweet
The flask was too clean to grow anything
quiz.why: Boiling killed the microbes in the broth. The long curved neck stopped dust and microbes from reaching it. When the neck was tipped, microbes arrived and the broth turned cloudy.

open_questions.q: Why does idli batter in different kitchens have different microbes, and does that change the taste?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have studied only a few kitchens. They do not yet know how much the microbes change from place to place or why.

open_questions.q: How much do the bacteria in our gut change our health and our mood?
open_questions.why_open: Studies often find links, but it is hard to tell which comes first. Many results have not yet been repeated.

open_questions.q: How did the first people discover that a spoon of curd makes more curd?
open_questions.why_open: No written records survive from that time. Archaeologists have found traces of fermented food that are thousands of years old, but not how it began.

open_questions.q: How do yeast and bacteria sense and signal to each other?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have found chemical signals between bacteria, called quorum sensing. They are still learning how much of this goes on in food.

open_questions.q: Could microbes in soil and compost help us grow food without chemicals?
open_questions.why_open: Early results are promising, but scientists are still finding out which microbes help and which do harm.

open_questions.q: Are there microbes no one has ever found?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists think most microbes on Earth have never been grown in a laboratory, so they have not been described.
