maths.problem: A balloon on a bottle of yeast, sugar and warm water measures 4 cm around at 10 minutes, 9 cm at 20 minutes, 15 cm at 30 minutes and 22 cm at 40 minutes. If it grows by the same amount in the next 10 minutes as it did in the last 10 minutes, how big will it be at 50 minutes?
maths.explain: From 30 to 40 minutes it grew 22 minus 15, which is 7 cm. Adding 7 cm to 22 cm gives 29 cm. This is a guess from the line on the graph.
maths.context: In the Yeast Balloon test, you measure a balloon every 10 minutes and draw a line graph.
maths.why_maths: A line graph lets you see how fast something grows, and make a sensible guess about what comes next.

maths.problem: A bacterium in warm milk splits into two every hour. You start with 5 bacteria. How many are there after 5 hours?
maths.explain: The number doubles each hour. 5 becomes 10, then 20, then 40, then 80, then 160. That is 5 times 32, because doubling five times is multiplying by 32.
maths.why_maths: This shows how quickly a small number of microbes can become a very large number, which is why a spoon of starter is enough to set a whole pot of milk.

maths.problem: A dosa batter recipe uses 4 cups of rice for every 1 cup of dal. You have 2 cups of dal. How many cups of rice do you need to keep the same ratio?
maths.explain: You have 2 times as much dal as the recipe. So you need 2 times as much rice. 2 times 4 is 8.
maths.why_maths: A ratio keeps the batter the same, however much you make. The right mix of rice and dal gives the right stickiness to hold the gas.

maths.problem: A recipe says to use 1 teaspoon of starter curd for every 250 millilitres of milk. How many teaspoons do you need for 2 litres of milk? One litre is 1000 millilitres.
maths.explain: 2 litres is 2000 millilitres. 2000 divided by 250 is 8. So you need 8 teaspoons of starter.
maths.why_maths: You need to know how much starter to add so that there are enough bacteria to set the milk, and not too many to make it sour too fast.

maths.problem: Milk with starter is left to set at 9:30 in the evening. It takes 9 hours and 15 minutes to set. At what time is the curd ready?
maths.explain: From 9:30 pm, 9 hours later is 6:30 am. Then 15 more minutes makes 6:45 am.
maths.context: In the Curd Test, curd sets slowly, and you check it in the morning.
maths.why_maths: Fermenting takes hours. Working out when it will be ready tells you when to check, so you do not disturb the cups too soon.

maths.problem: Batter was 6 cm high at 8 in the evening, and 9 cm high at 8 the next morning. By what fraction of its starting height did it rise? Write it in its simplest form.
maths.explain: It rose 9 minus 6, which is 3 cm. 3 out of 6 is 3 over 6. Both numbers divide by 3, so 3 over 6 is 1 over 2, one half.
maths.context: In Batter Watch, you mark the batter's height at the start and measure it again in the morning.
maths.why_maths: A fraction of the starting height tells you how much the batter rose, whatever the size of the jar.

maths.problem: Five friends each did the Curd Test at home. The bar chart shows, for each cup, in how many homes the curd had set by the morning. Cups B and D were kept in the same place, but only B had a starter. In how many more homes did cup B set than cup D?
maths.explain: The bar for cup B is 4 and the bar for cup D is 0. 4 minus 0 is 4. B and D were kept in the same place, so the difference comes from the starter.
maths.context: In the Curd Test, cup A is warm, cups B and D are on the counter, and cup C is in the fridge. Only D has no starter.

chart.title: Homes where the curd had set by morning (out of 5)

maths.why_maths: A bar chart shows at a glance which cups set. Comparing two bars that differ in only one way shows which thing mattered.

maths.problem: Louis Pasteur showed in 1857 that living microbes make milk turn sour. How many years before 2026 was that?
maths.explain: 2026 minus 1857 is 169. First 2026 minus 1800 is 226. Then 226 minus 57 is 169.
maths.why_maths: Subtracting dates shows how long people have known an idea, and how new some of our knowledge of microbes still is.

how_we_found_out.story: For thousands of years, people made bread, curd and wine without knowing how it worked. In the 1830s, many scientists, including the famous German chemist Justus von Liebig, taught that fermentation was just chemistry. They said sugar fell apart as it rotted, and no living thing was needed. Louis Pasteur, a French chemist, did not agree. In 1857 he looked at fermenting milk under a microscope and saw tiny living things, which he said made the acid. In 1860 he showed that yeast cells grew and multiplied as sugar fermented. Then he boiled a sugar broth in a flask with a long, curved neck. Dust and microbes could not climb in, and the broth stayed clear for months. When he tipped the neck, microbes arrived and the broth turned cloudy. This showed that fermentation needs living microbes.
how_we_found_out.who: Louis Pasteur, a French chemist (1822 to 1895)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Many scientists thought fermentation was only chemistry, a kind of rotting with nothing alive in it. Pasteur showed that it stopped when the microbes were killed, and began again when they were let back in.

playtest: Read as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, but not yet cooked or tested at home. Yeast Balloon: the cold bottle stays in the fridge, because a bottle left on the counter would warm up and catch up. The quantities (200 millilitres, one teaspoon of yeast and two of sugar) and the 40 minutes are from the usual home version of this test, and the balloon sizes in the maths question are a made-up example, not measured. Curd Test: in a hot kitchen cups A and B may look alike, so the steps say to write exactly what you see. Cup D is never tasted. Make Idli: the soak, grind, rest and steam times follow a standard home recipe. The batter must be ground at least 8 hours before steaming. The videos have no address yet. Feasibility review: balloon sizes and the time to start swelling (about 15 to 20 minutes) are typical and not promised; family trials are still needed for the yeast quantities, the oven-light warmth and the curd timings. Facts were read against the sources list, and two details should be checked by a person before the unit goes live: that the oven light alone keeps a typical home oven near 35 to 40 degrees, and the Hindustan Antibiotics start year (1954).
